newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Volvo's Gyll denies power struggle report.
newsitem.headline: Volvo's Gyll denies power struggle report.

text.p: Volvo Corp chief executive Soren Gyll denied on Friday a magazine report that there was a boardroom power struggle going on in the company.

In a front-page interview with business daily Dagens Industri, the contents of which were later confirmed to Reuters, Gyll said the Swedish vehicle manufacturer was concerned about the process of transformation now underway.

"There's been a good deal of tension in Volvo's management, but we're now more unified than we have been for a long time," Gyll said in the article, whose banner headline read: "Fear and Worries at Volvo -- Soren Gyll speaks out on rumours, power struggles and turbulence at Volvo.".
Swedish business magazine Veckans Affarer said earlier this week that Gyll had squabbled with Volvo board chairman Bert-Olof Svanholm several times in boardroom meetings.
A Volvo spokesman confirmed Gyll's comments in Dagens Industri.

Volvo's transformation from what was effectively a holding company to an out and out automotive group had given rise to a new corporate culture, Gyll said, adding that the employees now had far more responsibility than in the past.
"A lot of people will certainly find this tough," Gyll said.
Gyll said the realisation that Volvo was now entirely dependent on vehicles for its survival had come as a shock to many employees.
He said the company would need to use synergies available to it to cut costs by around 30 percent by the end of the decade.
"I estimate that by coordination between a number of areas in the group, we can cut costs by several hundred million crowns," Gyll said.
Many industry analysts believe that Volvo's volumes are too low in its car operations and that the unit cannot tolerate excessive R&D costs.
Gyll emphasised that cost-cutting in connection with major marketing investments will return the company to healthy profitability.
"We will return to satisfactory long-term profitability, and will be making new decisions around the end of October to achieve this," he said.
